persons.name: Usama Bin Ladin

events.description: Bin Ladin moved to Afghanistan after abrupt departure from Sudan; finances became harder to track.
US Embassy bombings increased al-Qa'ida's need for security, pushing finances underground.
UN Security Council Resolution 1333 passed late in the year, calling on states to freeze funds associated with al-Qa'ida.
CTC intelligence report 'Pursuing the Bin Ladin Financial Target' issued.
Bin Ladin moved to Afghanistan, after which al-Qa'ida's financial activities went underground.
Bin Ladin's abrupt departure from Sudan, reportedly forced to liquidate most of his assets at a loss.
The UN Security Council passed Resolution 1333, calling for member states to freeze funds associated with al-Qa'ida (described as 'late last year').
CTC issued the intelligence report 'Pursuing the Bin Ladin Financial Target'.
The Saudi Government froze Bin Ladin's bank accounts in the Kingdom and his interest in his family's construction business.

key_claims: Bin Ladin's funds are hard to track because he uses hawala dealers, couriers, banks and NGOs forming a network with few long-lasting nodes.
Al-Qa'ida moved its finances underground after the US Embassy bombings and the Sudan liquidation.
NGOs are exploited because legitimate humanitarian funds are co-mingled with funds for terrorism.
Bin Ladin's income sources are diversified (NGOs, donors, investments, commercial activities, drug trafficking), so removing one or two would not appreciably reduce capability.
Key hawala dealers and money changers in Pakistan support al-Qa'ida money movement.
CIA lacks reporting to estimate Bin Ladin's net worth, personal wealth use or family support.
UNSCR 1333 will likely make Bin Ladin and associates more discreet.
